slot.topic_title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

item.title: Setting Up a Test for Streetlight Outages
item.stimulus: A city reports that 10% of its 9,400 streetlights are out of service. After a new repair program, the city's public works department believes that the proportion of the city's streetlights that are out of service has decreased. An inspector checks a random sample of 120 of the city's streetlights and finds that 9 of them are out of service. The department plans to use these data to test its belief.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate testing procedure, and define the parameter of interest in context.

criteria.text: Names a one-sample z-test for a population proportion.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies a one-sample z-test for a (single) population proportion; naming a test for a mean or a two-sample procedure does not earn the point.
criteria.fix: With one sample and a yes-or-no response, name the procedure as a one-sample z-test for a population proportion.

criteria.text: Defines p as the proportion of all the city's streetlights that are out of service (after the repair program).
criteria.evidence: Response defines the parameter as a proportion that refers to all of the city's streetlights and to being out of service, not to the 120 sampled lights or the count of 9.
criteria.fix: Define p with three pieces: a proportion, the response (out of service), and the population (all of the city's streetlights).

parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for the department's test.

criteria.text: H₀: p = 0.10 (or H₀: p ≥ 0.10, tested at 0.10) and Hₐ: p < 0.10.
criteria.evidence: Response writes the null hypothesis at the value 0.10 (p = 0.10, or p ≥ 0.10 as the CED permits for a one-sided test) and a one-sided alternative p < 0.10, both in terms of the population proportion p (not p̂).
criteria.fix: Put the status quo value in H₀ with an equals sign and the department's belief (a decrease) in Hₐ using <.

parts.prompt: Verify the randomization condition and the 10% condition for this test.

criteria.text: States that the randomization condition is met because the inspector checked a random sample of the city's streetlights.
criteria.evidence: Response cites the random sample of 120 streetlights as meeting the randomization condition.
criteria.fix: For the randomization condition, quote the random selection described in the study and say what was randomly selected.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met because 120 ≤ 0.10(9,400) = 940 (equivalently, 9,400 ≥ 10 × 120 = 1,200).
criteria.evidence: Response compares the sample size 120 with 10% of the 9,400 streetlights (or compares 9,400 with 10 × 120) and states the condition is met.
criteria.fix: Show the 10% condition with numbers: compare the sample size with 10% of the stated population size.

parts.prompt: A classmate says that the normality condition for this test is not met because only 9 of the sampled streetlights were out of service. Is the classmate correct? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the classmate is not correct because the test's normality condition uses the null value p₀ = 0.10: np₀ = 120(0.10) = 12 and n(1 − p₀) = 120(0.90) = 108 are both at least 10.
criteria.evidence: Response says the classmate is incorrect and checks the expected counts 12 and 108 using p₀ = 0.10, both at least 10.
criteria.fix: For a test, check the normality condition with expected counts np₀ and n(1 − p₀), not with the observed counts.

item.model_answer:
(a) The appropriate procedure is a one-sample z-test for a population proportion. Let p = the proportion of all the city's streetlights that are out of service (after the repair program).

(b) H₀: p = 0.10
Hₐ: p < 0.10

(c) Randomization: the inspector checked a random sample of 120 of the city's streetlights, so the randomization condition is met.
10% condition: the sample of 120 streetlights is less than 10% of the city's 9,400 streetlights, because 0.10 × 9,400 = 940 and 120 ≤ 940, so the condition is met.

(d) The classmate is not correct. In a significance test the normality condition is checked using the null value p₀ = 0.10, because the test assumes H₀ is true. The expected number of out-of-service lights is np₀ = 120(0.10) = 12 and the expected number in service is n(1 − p₀) = 120(0.90) = 108. Both are at least 10, so the normality condition is met.
item.verification_python:
n=120;N=9400;p0=0.10;x=9
assert abs(0.10*N-940)<1e-9 and n<=0.10*N
assert 10*n==1200 and N>=10*n
assert abs(n*p0-12)<1e-9 and abs(n*(1-p0)-108)<1e-9
assert n*p0>=10 and n*(1-p0)>=10
assert x<10
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

decisions.objection: rubric_points: Part (b), criterion b1 requires equality in H₀ and therefore rejects the valid alternative H₀: p ≥ 0.10 paired with Hₐ: p < 0.10. The supplied CE
decisions.reason: CED 3.5.B.2 allows an inequality in a one-sided null hypothesis, tested at the equality boundary. b1 now accepts H₀: p ≥ 0.10 with Hₐ: p < 0.10.
